summary: Describes the Terminal Access Controller Access-Control System Plus (TACACS+) protocol, widely used to provide device administration for routers, network access servers and other equipment through centralized servers. It documents the protocol as deployed and is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: TACACS+ lets a network device ask a central server who may sign in, what they may do, and what they did. The RFC describes how these exchanges work and warns that the protocol must run over a protected network.

questions: how does tacacs+ authenticate device administrators
subtitle: How network devices use a central server for authentication, authorization, and accounting.

tldr.problem: Network devices need a way to check administrator identities, decide which actions they may take, and record those actions centrally.
tldr.mechanism: TACACS+ sends authentication, authorization, and accounting exchanges over TCP. Each packet has a 12-byte header, and the body uses shared-secret-based obfuscation.
tldr.outcome: RFC 8907 documents the Device Administration subset of a deployed protocol and warns that its obfuscation is not modern encryption. The unit metadata says it is updated by RFC 9887.

today: RFC 8907 is Informational and documents an already deployed protocol rather than an Internet Standards Track specification. The unit metadata says it is updated by RFC 9887.

sections.title: What TACACS+ Is For
sections.content:
TACACS+ was designed as an Authentication, Authorization, and Accounting (AAA) protocol. This memo focuses on Device Administration: checking access to network devices, deciding which operations are allowed, and auditing those operations.

The protocol was previously described in an unstandardized document called “The Draft.” This Informational RFC clarifies the subset common to Device Administration implementations. It removes SENDPASS, omits normative descriptions of some legacy features, and deprecates forwarding requests to another daemon.
sections.plainLanguage: TACACS+ lets a network device ask a central server to check a user's identity and permissions. The server can also keep records of actions on the device.

sections.title: Packets, Sessions, and Connections
sections.content:
TACACS+ uses TCP, with server port 49 allocated for its traffic. A session is one authentication sequence, one authorization exchange, or one accounting exchange. Authorization and accounting use a request and reply; authentication may take several messages.

Every packet begins with a 12-byte header containing version, packet type, sequence number, flags, session ID, and body length. Clients use odd sequence numbers and servers use even ones. Single Connection Mode can multiplex sessions on one TCP connection if both sides agree.
sections.plainLanguage: Each TACACS+ packet has a 12-byte header that identifies its type and session. A device and server exchange packets over TCP, and may share one connection across sessions.

sections.title: Authentication Exchanges
sections.content:
Authentication checks who a user or other entity is. A client begins with a START packet. The server may ask for a username, password, or other information, and the client answers with CONTINUE. The server finishes with PASS, FAIL, or ERROR.

ASCII login may take several rounds; the memo recommends limiting username retries to three. PAP, CHAP, and MS-CHAP login use a single START and REPLY. If a server marks a requested answer as sensitive with NOECHO, the client must not display it while the user types.
sections.plainLanguage: For a multi-step sign-in, the server can ask for information and the client returns it. The server then reports whether authentication passed, failed, or encountered an error.

sections.title: Authorization, Accounting, and Privileges
sections.content:
Authorization decides what a user may do. The client sends one REQUEST, and the server replies with approval, denial, or an error. Arguments can add conditions or options; a client must treat an unrecognized mandatory argument as a failed authorization.

Accounting records events such as a service starting, stopping, or continuing. A server must report success only after it records the request. For Device Administration, clients must send an accounting start record for every command entered. Privilege levels run from 0 to 15, with each level including the permissions of the next lower level.
sections.plainLanguage: Authorization tells the device which actions to allow. Accounting records what happened, including each entered command when the client supports Device Administration.

sections.title: Security Limits and Required Practices
sections.content:
The packet-body obfuscation uses MD5 and a shared secret, but provides no meaningful integrity, privacy, or replay protection. An attacker who can access the traffic should be assumed able to read and change packets. The RFC therefore says administrators must not rely on obfuscation.

TACACS+ must run on a network that protects privacy and integrity and is separated from other traffic. Servers must accept connections only from known clients, use shared secrets, and reject packets with the unencrypted flag. Servers and clients must support keys at least 32 characters long.
sections.plainLanguage: TACACS+ obfuscation does not stop an attacker from reading or changing traffic. The RFC requires a protected, separate network and says not to use the unencrypted option in production.
